sections.h2: Nebraska and capital gains on a home sale
sections.html:
Nebraska does not run a special capital gains schedule. Individuals fall under four ordinary bracket rates, and whatever part of your home-sale profit escapes the federal exclusion simply flows into the Nebraska return and is taxed at those rates.

The top rate drops to 4.55% for tax year 2026 from 5.20% in 2025. Many websites still print the older figure, so confirm the current one before you estimate your bill.

Two income tax layers sit on a sale: federal rules set the taxable gain, then Nebraska's brackets apply to what remains. A third charge, the documentary stamp tax, is a fee for transferring the deed and is not an income tax, so it appears in its own section further down.

Starting with tax years that begin on January 1, 2026, Nebraska uses four brackets at 2.46%, 3.51%, 4.55% and 4.55%. The Department of Revenue sets dollar limits for each filing status.

BracketRate (2026)Single filersMarried filing jointly
12.46%$0 to $4,130$0 to $8,250
23.51%$4,130 to $24,760$8,250 to $49,530
34.55%$24,760 to $39,900$49,530 to $79,800
44.55%Over $39,900Over $79,800

Standard deductions for 2026 are $8,850 single and $17,700 joint. Last year's schedule had a 5.01% third bracket and a 5.20% top bracket, which means the year your sale closes changes the math. The state's rate chronology lists every earlier year.

sections.h2: How much gain the IRS lets you skip
sections.html:
If the house was your primary residence, federal income tax can often skip $250,000 of the profit, or $500,000 for spouses filing together. The IRS explains the rules in Topic 701 and Publication 523.

Two tests decide it. Ownership: you held title for 24 months inside the five-year window that ends on closing day. Use: you lived there for 24 months inside that window. The months need not match.

  • Married couples: one spouse satisfying the ownership test is enough, yet each spouse must satisfy the use test.
  • Took the exclusion on another house within the last two years? You generally cannot take it again.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence community personnel on qualified extended duty can elect to pause the five-year window, up to 10 years.

Profit beyond the exclusion is what ends up on your returns, and it is taxed under both the federal and the Nebraska rates.

sections.h2: Federal rates on the taxable part
sections.html:
After a holding period over one year, federal net capital gain is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on taxable income. IRS Topic 409 gives the thresholds, which move annually. Using 2025 figures, the 0% rate covers income to $48,350 for singles, $96,700 for joint filers and $64,750 for heads of household. The 15% rate then reaches $533,400, $600,050 and $566,700 respectively, and anything higher is taxed at 20%.

One year or less makes it a short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income. Depreciation you claimed during a rental period can push that slice to as much as 25%. Large investment income may also bring the net investment income tax (IRS Topic 559).

A loss brings no deduction. The IRS counts a loss on your own home as personal, so it cannot be claimed.

Living elsewhere does not excuse you from a Nebraska return when you sell Nebraska property. Nebraska taxes nonresidents on Nebraska-source items, among them income, gain, loss and deductions that arise from owning or selling real property here.

People caught by this include:

  • Owners who left, rented the house, and then sold.
  • Heirs in other states who inherit a Nebraska house and sell.
  • Former residents who moved mid-year and sold in that same year and may be part-year residents.

The nonresident return is Form 1040N, and a Nonresident Income Tax Agreement form exists as well. Settle your filing status ahead of closing, either with the Department of Revenue or with a tax pro, since the sale may be your only Nebraska income that year.

Profit means the sale price minus adjusted basis. An inherited house gets its basis from special rules, not from the decedent's purchase price. Publication 551 deals with property received through gift or inheritance, and Topic 703 notes that improvements can add to basis.

An heir's profit, if any, turns on that figure. Keep proof of what the home was worth at death: an appraisal, estate inventory or county assessment record all work.

Nebraska inheritance tax is a different animal. It stands apart from income tax and is charged to whoever receives the property. Classes and rates are laid out in our Nebraska estate and inheritance tax guide.

The seller carries the documentary stamp tax, due when the deed is recorded. Value is counted in $1,000 units, with any leftover fraction rounded up to a full unit, at $3.32 a unit for deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later. Before then the unit price was $2.32. The register of deeds in the county takes payment.

Recording also needs a completed Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, submitted by the buyer or the buyer's agent (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-214). Some transfers carry no stamp tax:

  • Deeds between spouses or parent and child where nothing real is paid.
  • Distribution deeds from a personal representative to heirs or devisees.
  • Transfer on death deeds.
  • Foreclosure-avoidance deeds that secure or release a debt.

A normal sale to an unrelated buyer gets no exemption. Request the dollar figure from your title company ahead of time.

Received a Form 1099-S? Then the sale goes on your return, even if the gain is fully excludable, and it goes there too if only part of the gain is excludable. Use Form 8949 and Schedule D.

Taxable profit can also trigger quarterly estimated payments, which Publication 505 covers. A spring closing followed by a settle-up the next April risks an underpayment penalty, so ask your preparer about paying before year end.

If the buyer pays you over several years under an installment contract, you generally use the installment method unless you elect out. The home sale exclusion remains available in that setup.

• Note your purchase date and price, and collect every improvement receipt.
  • Verify 24 of the last 60 months as your residence.
  • Compare the 2026 and 2025 Nebraska schedules if rate changes touch your closing year.
  • Ask whether an heir or out-of-state owner must file in Nebraska.
  • Work the $3.32 per $1,000 stamp tax into closing costs for deeds recorded from July 18, 2026.
  • Hand your preparer the 1099-S and the settlement statement together.

This is not tax advice, and a Nebraska CPA or enrolled agent can run your own numbers. A house in rough shape can still sell: Cash Home Buyers makes as-is cash offers, so you can plan the tax side before you commit.

faqs.q: What is the Nebraska capital gains tax rate for 2026?
faqs.a: There is no separate rate. Taxable gain runs through the individual brackets, which are 2.46%, 3.51%, 4.55% and 4.55% for 2026.

faqs.q: Do I owe Nebraska tax if I sell my main home?
faqs.a: Only if gain is left after the federal exclusion of up to $250,000, or $500,000 for a joint return. Excluded gain stays out of income, though a Form 1099-S still means you report the sale.

faqs.q: How long must I live in the house to use the exclusion?
faqs.a: Own it and live in it for at least 24 months each during the five years before you sell. The two 24-month periods can fall at different times.

faqs.q: Does Nebraska tax a nonresident who sells a house in the state?
faqs.a: Yes. Income and gain tied to Nebraska real property are taxable for nonresidents, who file Form 1040N.

faqs.q: Who pays the Nebraska documentary stamp tax?
faqs.a: The seller, as grantor, pays when the deed is recorded with the register of deeds. For deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026 the rate is $3.32 per $1,000 of value.
